A market is a group of buyers and sellers of a good or service, together with the arrangement through which they trade. What is a market? Marginal Falls: Apartment rental market, Labor market, Farmers’ Market, Amazon

In analyzing markets, economists often begin with three assumptions: 1. People are rational. 2. People respond to incentives. 3. Optimal decisions are made at the margin. Assumptions about Economic Agents
• Rational agents use all information available at their disposal. Rationality • Rational agents weigh the benefits and costs of each action and try to make the best decision possible.
• An incentive is something that changes the benefit or cost of an action. Incentives • As incentives change, so do the actions that people will take.

When the price Forensics increases, two things happen: 1. Substitution Effect Forensics become more expensive relative to Detectives. 2. Income Effect The same budget can now buy less than before. Two Forces Behind the New Choice

In some markets, there are only a few firms. Each firm is large enough to affect the market. Each firm must watch what the others do. A New Kind of Market Oligopoly: A market structure with a small number of interdependent firms.

Perfect competition: One seller is too small to matter. Monopoly: One seller has no rival. Oligopoly: Each firm has rivals, and those rivals matter. Why Oligopoly is Different? Oligopoly = market power + strategic interaction
Oligopolies exist because entry is difficult. Common barriers: economies of scale control of key inputs government licenses patents large startup costs

Some industries require large fixed costs before production begins. Once the system exists, serving more customers becomes cheaper per customer. Large firms can spread fixed costs over many buyers. Small firms cannot. Economies of Scale
Entry can also be blocked by: Key input: one or few firms control what is needed. License: only approved firms can operate. Patent: legal protection prevents copying. Other Barriers to Entry

A game has: Players: who makes decisions. Strategies: what each player can choose. Payoffs: what each player gets from every combination of choices. For oligopoly: Players = firms Strategies = prices, output, advertising, quality Payoffs = profits What is a Game?
